vignette:
The Weight of Blueprints

Maya is twenty-four years old, a junior urban planner at a mid-sized city consultancy, and she is very good at designing spaces that feel safe. Her colleagues admire the careful way she considers sightlines, lighting, the placement of benches — the small details that make a public space feel welcoming rather than threatening. What they don't know is that she learned what danger feels like from the inside of a home.

Growing up in a tight-knit Vietnamese-Australian community in the western suburbs of Melbourne, Maya was raised primarily by her father after her mother returned to Vietnam when Maya was four. Her father worked long hours at a restaurant and drank heavily when he came home. From the time she was around six until she left for university at eighteen, he beat her — with his hands, occasionally with a belt — most often when she had done something he decided was shameful: a poor grade, a messy kitchen, a tone of voice he didn't like. Her grandmother lived with them for several years and said nothing. The community said nothing. Maya learned to read her father's footsteps on the front path, the particular sound the key made in the lock when he was drunk, the way silence in the house could be either safety or the thing right before danger.

She left for university and told herself she had left all of it behind. For a few years, that felt almost true. She threw herself into her degree, made friends, discovered she had a genuine passion for urban design. But in her second year of working, something shifted. A supervisor — a large man with a loud voice — began criticising her work in team meetings, leaning over her desk to point at her drawings. He never touched her. He was not, by any objective measure, threatening. But Maya's body did not make that distinction. Her heart would slam against her ribs. Her vision would narrow. She would find herself sitting very still, the way she used to sit at the dinner table, waiting for something to pass.

She started arriving at the office early to avoid him, then staying late. She began checking her work obsessively before any meeting, convinced that a mistake would trigger something she couldn't name. At night she dreams of her childhood bedroom — not always the same dream, but always the same feeling of being cornered, of the door being the wrong distance away. She wakes at three or four in the morning and cannot go back to sleep. She lies in the dark cataloguing sounds: the building settling, a car outside, a neighbour's television. Her body insists there is something to prepare for.

She has pulled away from most of her friends over the past year. Socialising requires a kind of ease she no longer has access to. She cancels plans and then feels ashamed of cancelling, which makes her less likely to make plans at all. She has not told her father what his behaviour did to her. She calls him occasionally because not calling feels like a different kind of wound, and the conversations are brief and careful, conducted in a register she developed as a child: pleasant, non-committal, watchful.

What troubles Maya most is not the nightmares or even the hypervigilance — it is the way she has started to feel like a stranger to herself. She chose urban planning because she wanted to build environments where people could move through the world without fear. She believes in that work. But she sits at her drafting table some mornings and feels the distance between the person who cares about that and the person she has become — someone who flinches at raised voices, who cannot quite trust that a room is safe even when every rational signal says it is. She is beginning to wonder, quietly and with some courage, whether she deserves the same careful attention she gives to the spaces she designs for other people.
